sweep_summary: Two title-sweep items: Downing 2004 (ZASPiL 37, open at zaspil.leibniz-zas.de, fetched sources/read) reports Tucker 1994 p. 18 — Dholuo stress on the stem-initial vowel, morphologically determined, unmoved by affixes — which confirms the catalog's 'morphological' coding; Schiller 1982 is a history dissertation on two Luo polities 'under stress' (Glottolog/EBALL record only), not relevant. From files already on file I also read Oduor 2002 (UoN PhD, first-hand): a weight-based account — stress on the last heavy syllable, penultimate in V-final and final in C-final words utterance-finally, diagnosed by vowel doubling; her review reports Omondi 1982 (root-syllable stress), Stafford 1967 and Odhiambo 1981 (penultimate). Blount 1969 (after Gregersen 1961:40) says regular penultimate stress. Best first-hand statement read: Oduor 2002 p. 163; it refines/competes with but does not supersede Cable 2009/Tucker 1994. Nothing left unread that needs acquiring from the item list; Tucker 1994 itself and Nimura 1996 (UoN thesis, no open file) remain the unobtained primary sources. Glottolog and Crossref were queried by curl instead.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Dholuo is detected towards the end of an utterance, through vowel doubling. Stress therefore has the effect of doubling Dholuo vowels. In a vowel final word stress is detected on the penultimate syllable and in a consonant final word, stress is detected on the last syllable. This stress pattern is what Okombo (1982) calls root lengthening (see section 1.7.2.2.4 above). [...] The discussions of stress in Dholuo words, in sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3, also show that stress is on the penultimate syllable in words ending in a vowel and on the last syllable in words ending in a consonant.
new_statements.citation: Oduor, Jane Akinyi Ngala. 2002. A study of syllable weight and its effects in Dholuo phonology. PhD thesis, University of Nairobi (hdl 11295/18409)
new_statements.reading: The only first-hand primary source read this sweep. Oduor (native-speaker linguist, KSN dialect) analyses Dholuo stress as quantity-sensitive: primary stress on the last heavy syllable, surfacing as penultimate in vowel-final and final in consonant-final words when utterance-final, cued by vowel doubling (= Okombo's root-lengthening). Her data are largely reconcilable with the catalog's root-initial (morphological) account — prefixed a-par/a-dek are stressed on the root, most disyllables initially — but her stated generalisation is positional/weight-based, not morphological, and her heaviness criterion is partly the stress cue itself. Downing 2004 (pp. 109-110, reporting Tucker 1994 p. 18: stress on the stem-initial vowel, morphologically determined, immobile under affixation) directly confirms the catalog's 'morphological' coding; Blount 1969 (after Gregersen 1961:40) and Stafford 1967 (via Oduor p. 68) give 'penultimate'. Net: the catalog's coding stands, with Oduor 2002 and the Gregersen/Stafford line worth recording as competing positional analyses.

audit.recode_to: Likely phonological, quantity-sensitive, right-edge: main stress on the last heavy (VV / lengthened) syllable = penult in vowel-final words, final in consonant-final words, initial default in all-light words (Okoth-Okombo 1982; Oduor 2002 ch. 4, 2015b, 2017); drop the Cable-only 'trochaic L-to-R alternating secondary stress' srule (no primary source states it). Keep a note that Tucker 1994 / the 1921 handbook describe the same facts as root-anchored (accent stays under encliticization), so final adjudication of morphological vs phonological should be made with Tucker 1994's stress section in hand; at minimum re-read with Oduor 2002 and add it as a contra source.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quotes verified verbatim at the stated places in the held Cable 2009 (p. 9), Swenson 2015 (pp. 104, 138) and SPA 1979/Gregersen files. (2) But the deciding source is a hedged 9-page course handout relaying Tucker 1994; the alternating-secondary-stress foot analysis is Cable's own and appears in no primary description. (3) The primary phonological literature by a native-speaker phonologist (Oduor 2002 PhD, fetched sources now, ch. 4 and pp. 278-279; Oduor 2017 p. 53, already held but unused; Okombo 1982:25 as quoted in held Ngala 1994) describes Dholuo stress as weight-driven and right-edge oriented (penult in V-final, final in C-final words; last heavy syllable; initial in all-light words, including on a prefix in a-jo-re), realized by utterance-final vowel doubling, and defines the 'root vowel' positionally. That is a different 'kind' from our 'morphological, root-initial' coding, even thou

sources.quote: p. 163: "Stress in Dholuo is detected towards the end of an utterance, through vowel doubling. Stress therefore has the effect of doubling Dholuo vowels. In a vowel final word stress is detected on the penultimate syllable and in a consonant final word, stress is detected on the last syllable. This stress pattern is what Okombo (1982) calls root lengthening"; p. 117: "section 4.2 and 4.3 show that stress falls on the last heavy syllable in Dholuo"; p. 104: "Most bisyllabic Dholuo words have stress on their first syllable."; p. 66 quoting Omondi 1982:21: "Dholuo word-roots are monosyllabic. Stress is fixed and it falls on the root syllable of the word."
sources.note: First-hand metrical (weight-based) analysis, KSN dialect: primary stress on the last heavy syllable; diagnosed by utterance-final vowel doubling, so it lands on the penult in V-final words and the final in C-final words (= Okombo's 'root-lengthening'); most disyllables (incl. verbs tedo) stressed initially, but prefixed a-par 'ten', a-dek 'three' stressed on the second (root) syllable; plural-imperative suffix -uru stressed on its first syllable. Also reports the earlier literature: Omondi 1982 (fixed root-syllable stress), Stafford 1967 (penultimate, immobile under suffixation, except -uru),…

sources.citation: Blount, Ben G. 1969. Acquisition of language by Luo children. PhD, University of California, Berkeley (ERIC ED038641). Appendix A 'An outline of Luo grammar'
sources.quote: 3. Suprasegmentals: a. stress: falls regularly on the penultimate syllable with secondary stress on geminate vowels (Gregersen 40), b. tone: (1) high tone does not occur in an unaccented syllable except after midtone. (2) stressed ultimate syllables contain only low tone. (3) complex tones occur only in a stressed penultimate syllable (41).
sources.note: Second-hand summary of Gregersen 1961 (Luo: a grammar), p. 40: regular penultimate stress, secondary stress on geminate vowels; tone restrictions keyed to stressed penult/ultima. A positional (penultimate) statement, at odds with the root-initial account but consistent with the CVCV canon where root = penult.

sources.citation: Downing, Laura J. 2004. What African languages tell us about accent typology. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 37: 101-136. doi 10.21248/zaspil.37.2004.247
sources.quote: However, Dholuo (E. Nilotic) is described by Tucker (1993) as having stress as well as tone. Stress is assigned to the stem-initial vowel. (That is, stress placement is determined by morphological, not phonological, position.) When a word is in phrase-final position, the stressed vowel is noticeably lengthened, at least in some dialects. [...] Since stress is morphologically determined, words of identical lengths but different morphological structures will be stressed on different syllables, as shown in (6a). And adding suffixes does not change the position of stress away from the stem vowel, as shown in (6b). (6) Dholuo stress (Tucker 1993, p 18) [...] (a) ra+hî 'cobra' vs rawo 'hippo' (b) ra+hí+nì 'this cobra' vs. rawo+ni 'this hippo'
sources.note: Survey chapter (second-hand, reporting Tucker 1993/1994 p. 18): Dholuo has stress plus tone; stress is fixed on the stem-initial vowel, i.e. morphologically determined, unaffected by prefixes or suffixes; the stressed vowel is lengthened phrase-finally in some dialects. Groups Dholuo with Lango, Dinka, Shilluk as Nilotic 'morphemic stress' languages.
